extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in information technology, NLP/ML, and fact-checking working on health/medical misinformation on social media
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive survey of information-technology approaches (manual and automatic) to detect, verify, and mitigate health-related misinformation in social networks, including datasets, features, models, and open challenges. Targets methods using content, propagation, and source features and their combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensions for understanding fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is understood by considering the dimensions of authenticity, intention, and news content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity: whether factual claims are valid. Intention: whether there is intent to deceive. News/content: whether the item is news (in social media this may be unclear). Use these three dimensions to distinguish misinformation, disinformation, malinformation, satire, parody, propaganda, hoaxes, rumors, and clickbaits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology distinctions (misinformation/disinformation/malinformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term misinformation characterizes both intentionally and unintentionally false or misleading information; disinformation is false information purposely spread to deceive; malinformation is deliberate dissemination of true information for harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctly labeling items (misinformation vs disinformation vs malinformation) is important for selecting detection and mitigation strategies; satire/parody and advertising/PR should also be recognized as distinct phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake news life-cycle in social networks
rubrics_metrics.description: The life cycle includes news creation, publishing on the network, and online propagation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define roles: author (originator), publisher (first poster on network; may be same as author), propagation (re-postings, retweets, comments, likes/upvotes). Detection and mitigation may target different phases (e.g., early detection during propagation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual vs automatic fact-checking tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual (expert or crowd) fact-checking offers accuracy but is slow and expensive; automatic approaches are necessary to handle scale and speed of social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine manual fact-checking with automatic systems: manual methods provide high-quality labels and datasets; automatic approaches focus on claim detection and scalable evidence retrieval/verification to complement manual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert-based fact-checking characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert-based fact-checking is done by domain experts and journalists, yielding accurate results but being expensive and time-consuming and difficult to scale to rapidly changing domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Politifact’s process and Truth-O-Meter ratings; expert selection of claims tends to focus on most significant claims. Use expert fact-checks to build high-quality datasets (e.g., FEVER, SciFACT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-O-Meter rating categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Politifact uses Truth-O-Meter ratings that classify claims into: True, Mostly True, Half True, Mostly False, False, and Pants on Fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categorical ratings are an example of human-annotated veracity labels; consider granularity and inter-annotator agreement when using such labels in datasets or evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd-sourced fact-checking characteristics and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd-sourced approaches enlist many volunteers to rate credibility; they are more economical but may introduce population biases and suffer from objectivity, evidence availability, and motivation issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of articles by the crowd may be unbalanced across topics/political spectrum; balancing and expert filtering of selection are important to reduce bias. Tools like Fiskkit allow sentence-level user ratings and tagging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual fact-checking workflow (monitoring, selection, research, rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The process consists of monitoring sources, selecting articles to check, researching claims using multiple sources, and assigning ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experts select claims they can balance coverage; when crowds select claims it is harder to ensure equitable coverage. Objectivity is challenged by non-expert raters and time-sensitive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic fact-checking pipeline: claim detection + claim validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic fact-checking consists of two steps: (a) detecting the claims in text, and (b) assessing the validity of the claims by retrieving evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both steps are challenging; claim detection must find check-worthy claims (often trending), and claim validation requires retrieving trustworthy evidence and applying verification models (e.g., NLI or knowledge-base checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check-worthiness and claim prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Most check-worthy claims are those for which people show interest and that are trending; social metadata like number of likes and reposts are used as features to identify top claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize claims using engagement signals and topic relevance. Relying only on crowd interest can bias towards sensational claims; combine signals for balanced prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-detection subtasks (claim sentence, claimer, claim object, stance, boundaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim detection involves multiple subtasks: identifying the claim sentence, the claimer (source), the claim object, the stance of the claimer, and exact claim boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include Claimbuster, NLI zero-shot classifiers, fine-tuned BERT for boundary detection, Semantic Role Labeling for claimer extraction; many of these tasks (especially claim sentence detection) remain difficult for current models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-processing requirements for content methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Before feature extraction, preprocess data using tokenization, lowercase transformation, removal of stop words, sentence segmentation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper preprocessing affects downstream features and model performance; maintain provenance of preprocessing decisions for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-based detection: feature categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Content-based methods extract features from text and related content including: text representations, linguistic features, emotional features, entity-based features, stylistic features, topic extraction, user-profile features, image-based features, and external features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features feed ML classifiers or neural architectures; Table 3 in the survey summarizes available features. Choose features appropriate to the medical domain (e.g., domain-specific entities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Models and architectures used for content approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Content features can be used with ML classifiers or concatenated/aggregated in neural networks such as FNNs, RNNs, CNNs, LSTMs, GANs, Seq2Seq (transformers), GNNs, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select architecture based on available data size, feature types, and multimodal needs; consider model complexity vs explainability in health contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim validation via evidence retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence retrieval is the task of retrieving documents (text, tables, KB facts, images, metadata) that support prediction of a claim; identifying trustworthy sources is fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use curated trustworthy sources (WHO, CDC, BMJ, MedlinePlus, etc.) as primary evidence pools; combine web search, domain-specific corpora (CORD-19), and scientific literature. Ranking and retrieval quality critically affect verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-verification using Natural Language Inference (NLI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification often leverages NLI to classify relationship between evidence (premise) and claim (hypothesis) as entailment, contradiction, or neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-verification systems must handle multiple evidence pieces found automatically; ensemble or graph-based approaches (e.g., KGAT) can offer finer-grained verification. NLI approaches require careful evidence selection to avoid hallucination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge-base (KB) / Knowledge-graph (KG) approaches for validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert textual claim to triples (subject, predicate, object) and check against KB/KG facts; KGs often use RDF/OWL representations and enable logical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KG methods must handle KB incompleteness (Open World Assumption). Use KG embeddings, path features, or rule-mining to validate claims; complement KGs with external resources when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to validate claims against incomplete knowledge bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Three main approaches: (a) complement KB with external web resources to find missing triples, (b) embedding-based and path-based approaches using graph embeddings or path properties, (c) rule-based approaches using rule mining for validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External extraction can be inaccurate; embedding methods verify unseen entity pairs statistically; rule-based methods are more interpretable. Combining embedding and rule-based approaches often yields better performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: knowledge sources are imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: Kgs and KBs (e.g., those derived from Wikipedia/DBpedia) are not fully accurate — e.g., DBpedia v3.6 ~80% correct; Wikipedia snapshots may contain false facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for source quality and temporal drift; validate claims with multiple independent trustworthy sources and track KG provenance and versioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation-based detection methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use propagation features and network structure (diffusion patterns, cascade shapes, temporal dynamics) to detect fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propagation features can help where content is informal or noisy; early-detection methods leverage propagation signals to limit spread. Structural contrasts between misinformation and true information can be exploited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-credibility / user-profile features
rubrics_metrics.description: Use features of publishers and users (credibility, history, network characteristics) as signals for detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profile features complement content and propagation signals; detect malicious instigators or coordinated actors (bots, trolls) and incorporate into mitigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal / fused approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news detection typically fuses content, propagation, and source features because both textual and structural information, user context, social context, and spatio-temporal info are useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fusing modalities improves detection: e.g., informal health-related content benefits from propagation and user-profile features, while formal medical content benefits from linguistic/medical features; popular content benefits from linguistic-emotional features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation objectives and approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigation techniques aim at early detection of fake news and limiting the spread, applied at propagation and source levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation strategies include recommending fact-checking URLs, blocking or downranking misinformation, and interventions targeting influential spreaders. Evaluate mitigation by reduction of spread and timeliness of intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Datasets standards and desirable properties
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality datasets should contain real-world claims, evidence (supporting and contradictory), veracity labels, and explanations/rationales; in-domain (medical) data improves model accuracy and explanation quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FEVER (SUPPORTED/REFUTED/NOTENOUGHINFO), SciFACT and SciFACT-Open for scientific claims, COVID-Fact and HealthVer (claims + evidence + contradictory claims), PubHealth (explanations). Construct datasets with careful retrieval/ranking of scientific papers and manual annotation of relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset labeling scheme example (FEVER)
rubrics_metrics.description: FEVER labels claims as SUPPORTED, REFUTED, or NOTENOUGHINFO based on evidence from Wikipedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose label granularity appropriate to downstream tasks; ensure annotator guidelines for evidence selection and rationales to improve reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health-specific dataset construction procedure (HealthVer example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step approach: (1) retrieve real-world claims from search snippets about COVID-19, (2) retrieve and rank relevant scientific papers from CORD-19 using a relevance model, (3) manually annotate relations between evidence statements and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pipeline emphasizes using real-world queries and human annotation to produce reliable evidence-labelled datasets for training and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training on in-domain data improves performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Training models on in-domain (medical/COVID) data greatly improves accuracy of veracity prediction and the quality of generated explanations compared to generic training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use domain-adaptive pretraining and continuous training on domain data (e.g., SciFACT, COVID-Fact) to transfer domain knowledge into pre-trained language models; this is particularly important for medical terminology and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation and difficulty of subtasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Many subtasks (claim sentence detection, claim object extraction, claimer detection, claim boundary detection) are difficult for current models; stance detection is particularly challenging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark performance per subtask, use specialized corpora (NewsClaims, PolNeAR), and consider multi-task or pipeline architectures. Report per-class metrics and error analysis to reveal weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of trustworthy site lists and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checking and evidence retrieval should prioritize trustworthy medical websites (WHO, CDC, BMJ, MedlinePlus, etc.) and track provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use curated lists (Table 1) as primary evidence sources; provenance, versioning, and authority ranking are important for reliable verification.
